$500K Retirement Sequence-of-Returns Risk & 24-Month SGOV Buffer

Drawing $20,000/yr from a $500K portfolio during a 50% equity drop sells twice as many shares; a $40K–$75K SGOV reserve prevents forced selling.

Quick Dollar Drawdown Estimator (2000–2025 Historical Data)

At a $500,000 nest egg paired with Social Security, a modest 4% annual withdrawal equals $20,000 a year ($1,667/month). In calm bull markets, that math feels effortless. The real danger arrives if a 2000 or 2008 downturn lands during years one through three of retirement.

Selling $20,000 of shares after a 50% drop removes the exact units needed for the subsequent recovery. Economists call this sequence-of-returns risk, and two households earning the exact same 25-year average return can end up hundreds of thousands of dollars apart solely because of early withdrawal timing.

Setting aside 24 to 36 months of withdrawals inside 0–3 month US Treasury bills (SGOV) lets a $500K household fund monthly transfers from cash reserves while allowing the SMH and XLV equity sleeves to recover untouched.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much cash reserve does a $500K household typically model?

At a $20,000/year gap above Social Security, 24 months equals $40,000 (8%) and 36 months equals $60,000–$75,000 (12–15%).
